bib.title: Machine Learning Engineering in Action, Chapter 13: ML development hubris

question: How do ML teams avoid unmaintainable, over-engineered code and technology choices driven by developer ego rather than the business problem?
contributions: Scale from under-engineered to over-engineered ML code, with phased development guidance
Five developer personas (Hacker, Mystic, Show-off, Mad Scientist, Good Samaritan) shown on one column-casting task
Guidance against premature generalization (custom frameworks) and premature optimization, with a runtime breakdown
Guidance on adopting alpha-stage open source tools and on solution-driven vs technology-driven development

results.claim: The author's rate of fixing imperative, tightly coupled Spark code before predictions lapsed after an upstream column change was under 40 percent.
results.metric: success rate fixing code after upstream data change
results.setup: Author's personal experience on imperative script-style ML jobs, not a controlled measurement
results.quote: My success rate for fixing things (adjusting the code base to support a fundamental change that happened upstream in the data) before the lack of new predictions became obvious and a problem was, at that time, just under 40%.

results.claim: Premature-optimised load-test data generator (Seq with positional lookup) scales worse than linear: 5,000 rows 0.6 s, 500,000 rows about 1 min 20 s, 50 million rows about 2 h 54 min.
results.setup: Scala/Spark dog dataset generator, listing 13.10; Seq used where IndexedSeq needed, O(n) access; hardware not stated
results.quote: Generating 5,000 rows takes about 0.6 seconds, while a heavy load testing of 500,000 rows takes around 1 minute and 20 seconds. With the full load test of 50 million rows, the idea of waiting around for 2 hours and 54 minutes is a bit much.
results.note: Later text says more than 174 minutes for the same run (2 h 54 min = 174 min)

results.claim: Refactored generator (listing 13.11) scales linearly: 50 million rows in about 15 minutes versus more than 174 minutes.
results.setup: Same generator, refactored to ArrayBuffer and groupBy; hardware not stated
results.quote: The 50 million target that was tested from the previous implementation, however, returns that row count in approximately 15 minutes. That’s quite a bit better than the more than 174 minutes from the earlier implementation.

results.claim: Fermi-level breakdown of ML training wall-clock time: about 90 percent on feature engineering/hyperparameter tuning-type stages; ingestion, casting and cleaning 5 percent; logging and registration 2 percent.
results.metric: share of wall-clock runtime by pipeline stage
results.setup: Figure 13.10, generic ML pipeline estimate, not measured; the figure values are 5%, 2%, 90%, 2%, and the text says most time goes to data ingestion manipulations and hyperparameter tuning
results.quote: As you can see, the vast majority of processing time for ML project code is primarily focused on data ingestion manipulations (loading data, joining data, calculating aggregations on data, and converting ordinal and categorical data to numeric representations) and hyperparameter tuning.
results.note: Figure labels and percentages are separated in the extracted text; the mapping of 5/2/90/2 to boxes is read from Fig 13.10 layout and is uncertain. The figure text itself says model training dominates runtime.

results.claim: Rule of thumb for building a custom framework: it must accelerate project work by at least twice the time spent building and maintaining it, and the team needs at least 16 human hours per week to maintain it.
results.quote: If you can’t devote at least 16 human hours per week to maintaining the framework, adding features, and troubleshooting it, you should reconsider whether it’s worthwhile to start.
results.note: The second threshold (at least twice the time) is in the same sidebar, p382

results.claim: A custom FP-growth variant took three months and gave a 40 percent runtime improvement, then needed rework when Spark was upgraded; the alternative path using the standard algorithm lets the team deliver an 8.7 percent sales lift sooner.
results.setup: Hypothetical story in Fig 13.12; three months of work
results.note: 8.7% sales lift appears in the figure as a quoted remark from another team; hypothetical

results.claim: Cost-benefit test for swapping algorithms: whether a small accuracy gain is worth a large increase in compute budget.
results.quote: Is 0.1% accuracy worth a 50-times increase in budget to run the model?

limits: No experiments; all numbers are illustrative or anecdotal from the author's experience.
Runtime figures for the data generator give no hardware, cluster size or repeat count.
Fig 13.10 runtime split is a Fermi estimate, not a measurement.
Examples are Scala/Spark; the advice is language-general but the code is not directly reusable for Python stacks.
The chapter intro lists build vs buy vs prior art; the text discusses it through the framework-ownership questions and Section 13.5 rather than a dedicated decision table.
Product names (Seldon, Horovod, MLflow, Hyperopt) reflect 2022 tooling and have dated.
practices: Build something only as complex as the problem needs, since people have to maintain the code (p354).
Prototype with minimal imperative code and move complexity into modules only as the project nears MVP and production (Fig 13.2, p364).

Phase development: prototype (imperative wireframe), development (wrap repeated code in functions, externalise constants), MVP/production (abstract into module classes, co-locate functionality, optimise for runtime) (Fig 13.2, p364).

Match tooling to scale: pandas rather than SparkML for thousands of rows; a Flask app in Docker rather than Kubernetes with Seldon for a few requests per minute; ARIMA on CPU rather than multi-GPU LSTM when ARIMA gets single-digit RMSE (p356-357).
Be explicit in type casts; do not default every unmatched column to String, since implicit defaults create fragile production failures (Listing 13.8, p378).
Write code for the team's skill level; if using advanced idioms, teach them with documentation, internal examples, training and pair programming rather than linking a style guide in a PR (p377).
Do not build a custom framework or wrapper at project start; build one only when a dozen similar projects define shared patterns or hundreds of models (e.g. XGBoost) justify it (Fig 13.9, p380-382).
Before building a framework ask team size, open-sourcing, buy vs open source alternative, dependency count, value (at least twice the effort), and whether it only wraps pandas or Spark (p381-382).
Optimise only after the code works end to end, target the longest-running stages first, use built-in constructs, and consider simpler algorithms when runtime is poor (p389).
Do not run business-dependent projects on alpha-stage open source packages; evaluate new tools on open datasets in isolated environments and revisit at 1.0 (p391-392).
Choose tools by scientific comparison on productivity, maintainability, stability and cost, ignoring hype (p392).
Do not write custom algorithm implementations unless a real need such as an SLA exists, and then commit to maintaining them for as long as the use case lives (p393-395).

terms.definition: the possession of excessive pride and self-confidence
persona who copies internet snippets, overuses mutable state and loops, producing fragmented patchwork code
persona who applies functional programming purist-style across the whole code base, with dense one-liners
persona who builds complexity for its own sake to appear skilled
well-intentioned advanced developer whose efficient, compact code is opaque to a less experienced team because it was not taught
concise, clean code written so that others can understand it; complex only if the need requires it
building a generic framework or wrapper before projects define the patterns it would serve
optimising parts of code in isolation before the whole works end to end, often on stages that do not dominate runtime
building a custom solution for notoriety or interest rather than to solve the business problem; contrasted with solution-driven development
